searches.note: The perRecord counts are a record's own searches; one more, on the decrees of Hermitage, Cornas, Condrieu and Château-Grillet, served Chave, Clape and Vernay together, so the records' reports give six, six and five. Five of the thirty one returned nothing on their question: the first Guigal search (too many terms), two on the Stérimberg legend (one in French, one in English), one on the dates of Guigal's founder, and one on the place of L'Ermite on the hill, which gave only the chapel's building in 1864, in one account, and its ownership by the house since 1919. One search was spent on the death of the Clape founder's son, for the people list. No WebFetch was tried. Sixteen searches of the share are left unspent.

method: The fragment was written with no web search at all, resting on the Codex's library and region records and on the writer's memory of two reference books; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, the strongest first: the founders and their years, the appellation decrees, the sites and soils, the making and its months, the label words and every beat of the story.

Every source the fragment listed (the Codex's own library and two unopened books) is replaced by pages a search returned, read: search; marked primary where the result came from the producer's own domain (guigal.com, jaboulet.com), the appellation body (vins-rhone.com, Inter Rhône) or the INAO's own specifications (extranet.inao.gouv.fr). No page of Chave, Clape or Vernay was reached.

A fact in two independent sources or one primary stands; a producer's own claim is hedged as its account; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A writer's own site (Wine With Seth, The Wine Cellar Insider, a critic's pages) was read as a lead and never cited. Facts the library states stand as the brief allows, except where a search contested them.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile (the lint refused recent vintages and hectares, now in words), no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches. The lint's one note left standing, the first grower of the village to bottle his own Cornas, is hedged by most accounts and rests on several sources.

tested: The founding of 1946 at Ampuis (the house's history page, Wikipedia, Fells, the Vienne Condrieu tourist office): confirmed.

The founder at Vidal-Fleury from 1924 at fourteen (the house's English and French history pages; one account says 1923, and the house's own timeline graphic 1928): the record keeps 1924 at fourteen, the house's text.

The founder's blindness and his son's taking charge in 1961 (the house's history: struck by a temporary but total blindness; Wikipedia and two profiles: the son took over at 17, one says 18): confirmed and the record now says sudden, total and temporary, by the house's account, and the son then in his teens.
La Mouline 1966, La Landonne 1978, La Turque 1985 (Decanter's Wine Legend, Wikipedia, the importer's sheets, GuildSomm): confirmed; one importer page that gives 1978 for La Mouline was discounted.
Vidal-Fleury bought in 1984 (Wikipedia and the library; the house says the early 1980s and one merchant 1980): kept as 1984 and left open.

La Mouline's site, soil and vines (the house's La Mouline page and sheet: terraces in the shape of a Roman amphitheatre, gneiss with light coloured silica soil and limestone loess, 89 per cent Syrah and 11 per cent Viognier, vines of 75 to 100 years by different pages): confirmed and the soil corrected.
The élevage (the house: 40 months on the current sheet, 42 on the 2012 and 2018 pages; others 38 to 42): now forty to forty two months by the house's sheets.

Co-fermentation of the Viognier (Decanter's Wine Legend and one profile: the two co-ferment in steel vats; the library and the Codex's Côte-Rôtie records): confirmed; picking the two together found nowhere and cut.
Château d'Ampuis bought in 1995 and the cooperage set up there in 2003 (the house's history): added.
The founder's dates (one search): no source gives his birth or death year, so he stays unnamed.

The rules: nobody living named (the son and grandson met in every result), no price, no score (critics' marks met in results, none carried), nothing volatile (a share of the appellation's output met in results, not carried), no judging superlative, British, no dash; both questions have one key, options of one kind and an explanation naming the nearest wrong option: sound.

changed.was: Côte-Rôtie was a small and struggling vineyard when the founder of this house, who had worked since boyhood in the cellars of the Ampuis merchant Vidal-Fleury, set up on his own in 1946. When he lost his sight in 1961, his son, then in his teens, took charge. The slope above the village was already told as a story: a lord of Maugiron, it is said, left one hillside to a fair daughter and one to a dark one, and the names Côte Blonde and Côte Brune stuck to rocks that truly differ. With the 1966 vintage the house bottled the old vines of La Mouline, on the Blonde, as a wine of their own, when Côte-Rôtie was almost always a blend of the whole slope. La Landonne followed in 1978 and La Turque in 1985, the trio the trade calls the La La wines, and in 1984 Guigal bought Vidal-Fleury, the house where its founder had begun. The three single vineyards carried the name of Côte-Rôtie far beyond the Rhône and helped bring abandoned terraces back into use. La Mouline remains the lesson in co-fermented Viognier: the white grape lends the perfume, the Syrah gives the frame.
changed.now: The founder of this house entered the cellars of the Ampuis merchant Vidal-Fleury in 1924, at fourteen, and set up on his own in 1946. In 1961, by the house's account, a sudden blindness, total though it proved temporary, struck him, and his son, then in his teens, took charge. The slope above the village was already told as a story: a lord of Maugiron, it is said, left one hillside to a fair daughter and one to a dark one, and the names Côte Blonde and Côte Brune stuck to rocks that truly differ. With the 1966 vintage the house bottled the old vines of La Mouline, on the Blonde, as a wine of their own. La Landonne followed in 1978 and La Turque in 1985, the trio the trade calls the La La wines, and in 1984 Guigal bought Vidal-Fleury, the house where its founder had begun. In 1995 it bought the Château d'Ampuis by the river, and in 2003 it set up its own cooperage there. The three single vineyards carried the name of Côte-Rôtie far beyond the Rhône. La Mouline remains the lesson in co-fermented Viognier: the white grape lends the perfume, the Syrah gives the frame.
changed.why: The house's history gives 1924 at fourteen and a sudden, total and temporary blindness in 1961, the Château d'Ampuis in 1995 and the cooperage in 2003; Côte-Rôtie small and struggling, almost always a blend in 1966, and abandoned terraces brought back were the writer's memory and found nowhere.

tested: The founding of 1834 by Antoine Jaboulet (1807 to 1864) at Tain, and the growth under his sons Paul and Henry (the house's history page; Justerini & Brooks: Paul gave his name to the business; The Wine Society: the elder of twin sons): confirmed; twins left out as one account.
The chapel of Saint-Christophe bought in 1919 (the house's timeline; Hachette Vins: owned by the house since 1919): confirmed; the vines around it and ownership in the present tense cut.
The sale of January 2006 to the Frey family (the library and several merchants): confirmed.

The label from 2021 (Berry Bros. & Rudd, The Drinks Business, Farr Vintners, Vinous, a Decanter column): from the 2021 vintage La Chapelle and the white are labelled Domaine de La Chapelle, not Paul Jaboulet Aîné, made in a winery of their own, still in the Frey family's hands; added to the label, the table, the story, a trap and the white's note.
The sites (several merchants' sheets: mainly Le Méal and Les Bessards, with Les Greffieux and Les Rocoules; granite at Les Bessards, pebbles at Le Méal and Les Rocoules): confirmed and widened.

The making (merchants' sheets and listings: fully destemmed, parcel by parcel, three to four weeks on the skins, twelve to eighteen months in French oak with 15 to 25 per cent new, a share in concrete eggs in the 2017 and 2021 listings): now in the record in words.

The legend (Inter Rhône's Hermitage page and Wikipedia: Gaspard de Stérimberg back from the Albigensian crusade, granted the hill by Blanche of Castile; 1224 in one telling and 1225 in another; the INAO, as reported, calls it apocryphal and the archives of Tain record hermits only from 1598): told as a legend in the 1220s. Two searches, one in French, returned nothing on it.
Blanche of Castile, 1188 to 1252 (Encyclopedia.com, Hérodote): confirmed.

The chapel (one search aimed at L'Ermite: Komoot gives the present chapel as built in 1864, a listed monument, the house's since 1919): the hermit now lives at the summit where a chapel now stands, rather than beside the chapel.

Hermitage in Bordeaux's clarets (Decanter's Battle of the Banks: Quai merchants strengthened claret with Hermitage; Justerini & Brooks: Bordeaux and Burgundy producers used it to strengthen their own; an English order of 1810 for claret with a dash of Hermitage): confirmed for the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

The rules: nobody living named (the Frey family kept as a family; the Jaboulet descendants never named), no price (Justerini & Brooks' line on the cost of Hermitage in the eighteenth century not carried), no score (marks met in the 2021 results, none carried), nothing volatile (recent vintages refused by the lint, now since the late 2010s), no judging superlative, British, no dash; questions sound.

changed.was: The hill takes its name from a legend: in 1224, the story goes, the knight Gaspard de Stérimberg came home from the crusade against the Albigensians, was granted the slope by Blanche of Castile (1188 to 1252) and lived out his days there as a hermit, beside the chapel at its summit. By the eighteenth century the wine of the hill was sold across Europe, and Bordeaux merchants blended it into their clarets for colour and body. The house began as a wine business at Tain in 1834 and took its name, Paul Jaboulet Aîné, from the founder's elder son. It came to own the chapel and the vines around it, and named its red Hermitage after it. Through the twentieth century La Chapelle was the Hermitage that drinkers abroad knew by name, and its 1961, with the 1978 beside it, became the measure of what northern Syrah can do with age. After a lean spell in the 1990s the family sold the house in 2006 to the Frey family, and the recovery of La Chapelle dates from that sale. When a guest names Hermitage, La Chapelle is often the wine they mean, and its old vintages show what the hill can become.
changed.now: The hill takes its name from a legend: in the 1220s, the story goes, the knight Gaspard de Stérimberg came home from the crusade against the Albigensians, was granted the slope by Blanche of Castile (1188 to 1252) and lived out his days there as a hermit, at the summit where a chapel now stands. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Bordeaux merchants strengthened their clarets with its wine, for colour and body. The house was founded at Tain in 1834 by Antoine Jaboulet (1807 to 1864) and grew under his sons Paul and Henry; it took its name from Paul, the elder. In 1919 it bought the chapel of Saint-Christophe, and its red Hermitage carries the chapel's name. Through the twentieth century La Chapelle was the Hermitage that drinkers abroad knew by name, and its 1961, with the 1978 beside it, became the measure of what northern Syrah can do with age. After a lean spell in the 1990s the family sold the house in 2006 to the Frey family, and the recovery of La Chapelle dates from that sale. With the 2021 vintage the wine moved to a label and a winery of its own, Domaine de La Chapelle. When a guest names Hermitage, La Chapelle is often the wine they mean.
changed.why: The legend's year differs between tellings (1224, 1225); the claret trade is dated to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by Decanter and Justerini & Brooks; the founder and his dates, his sons and the chapel of 1919 are the house's own history; the label and winery of 2021 are in three merchants' and the trade press.

tested: 1481 (the library, Decanter, the Wine Scholar Guild, several importers): confirmed as the family's own account.
The first Hermitage parcels bought in 1865 (Decanter's Wine Legend and two importers' pages): added.

The Hermitage appellation (the INAO's own specification: recognised by a judgment at Valence on 25 June 1936 and made a controlled appellation by the decree of 4 March 1937): confirmed as a decree of 1937.

The making (the Wine Scholar Guild, Grand Cru Selections and others: each plot picked and made apart, about a tenth new oak by two accounts, up to a fifth or more by others, the blend after some eighteen months, a total of about thirty months by one): the record says a small share of new wood and some eighteen months; the tasting of every lot before the blend was found nowhere and is cut.
Cuvée Cathelin (Decanter's Wine Legend, Hedonism, Wine Auctioneer): first made in 1990, only in chosen years, named for a painter friend of the family who drew its label, labelled Ermitage; added.

The Saint-Joseph terraces (Punch: the work began in 1995 above Mauves, with roads and rebuilt walls; Wine Spectator: the son took over in the early 1990s and then began reclaiming abandoned hillsides): the record says the 1990s.
Where the family's line began: Lemps appears only as a Saint-Joseph village of its holdings; left out.

The rules: nobody living named (the father and the son met in every result; the painter described, not named, for want of his dates), no price, no score, nothing volatile (counts of parcels and hectares met, none carried), no judging superlative, British, no dash; the two addresses that carry the son's name are kept out of the record; questions sound.

changed.was: By the family's own account its growers can be traced to 1481, and the vines have passed from father to son ever since. They worked the granite terraces of the west bank around Mauves, in what became the Saint-Joseph appellation, and came to hold parcels across the river on the hill of Hermitage. When the Hermitage appellation was drawn in 1937, the hill was already known by its climats, each with its own ground, from the granite of Les Bessards in the west to the lighter, stonier soils further east. Where some houses of the hill came to bottle their climats one by one, the Chaves held to the older idea of Hermitage as a blend of the whole slope, each parcel adding a voice: Bessards the frame, the eastern ground the perfume. The family also makes a white Hermitage that can outlast the red, a rare vin de paille of grapes dried on straw and, in chosen years, Cuvée Cathelin, a selection of the red. Late in the twentieth century it replanted abandoned Saint-Joseph terraces above Mauves. Chave's Hermitage makes the case for blending a hill rather than dividing it.
changed.now: By the family's own account its growers can be traced to 1481, and the vines have passed from father to son ever since. They worked the granite terraces of the west bank around Mauves, in what became the Saint-Joseph appellation, and in 1865 bought their first parcels across the river on the hill of Hermitage. When the Hermitage appellation was fixed by decree in 1937, the hill was already known by its climats, each with its own ground, from the granite of Les Bessards in the west to the stonier soils further east. Where some houses of the hill came to bottle their climats one by one, the Chaves held to the older idea of Hermitage as a blend of the whole slope, each parcel adding something the others lack. The family also makes a white Hermitage that can outlast the red, a rare vin de paille of grapes dried on straw and, from 1990 and only in chosen years, Cuvée Cathelin, a selection of the red. In the 1990s the son who had taken over the domaine began to reclaim abandoned Saint-Joseph terraces around Mauves. Chave's Hermitage makes the case for blending a hill rather than dividing it.
changed.why: 1865 in Decanter and two importers; the decree of 1937 in the INAO's specification; Cathelin from 1990 in Decanter and two merchants; the Saint-Joseph terraces from the 1990s in Punch and Wine Spectator, whose addresses carry a living name and stay in this review.

changed.was: Cornas faces Valence across the Rhône, and its name, it is said, comes from a Celtic word for burnt earth, for the sun on its granite terraces. The appellation was drawn in 1938, for red wine alone and Syrah alone. For decades most of the village's wine went in bulk to merchants, and the steep slopes, worked by hand, lost their growers to the fruit orchards of the plain. The grower whose name the domaine carries came to Cornas after the Second World War and began to bottle his own wine when few in the village did. He held to the old ways: whole bunches, no new wood, long months in big casks and vines tied to single stakes. His bottles found buyers abroad, and Clape became the address visitors sought when Cornas was barely known beyond the valley. He died in 2018, and his family has kept to the same methods, adding Renaissance from younger vines. Later growers who destem and buy new oak are measured against it: Clape's Cornas is the reference for traditional northern Syrah.
changed.now: Cornas faces Valence across the Rhône, and its name, it is said, comes from a Celtic word for burnt earth, for the sun on its granite terraces. The appellation was drawn in 1938, for red wine alone and Syrah alone. For much of the twentieth century most of the village's harvest was sold in bulk to merchants, and the steep slopes, worked by hand, lost their workers to the factories of the valley. The grower whose name the domaine carries, from a family of Languedoc vignerons, came to Cornas when he married into a family of growers there in 1949. For some years he too sold his wine in bulk; then, in the 1950s, he began to bottle it himself, by most accounts the first grower of the village to do so. He held to the old ways: whole bunches, concrete vats, no new wood and long months in old oval casks. He died in 2018, aged 93, and his son and grandson kept to the same methods. Growers who destem and buy new oak are measured against it, and Clape's Cornas is the wine to taste first to learn the traditional school of northern Syrah.
changed.why: The decree of 1938 is the INAO's; bulk sales for most of the century, the marriage of 1949, the bottling of the 1950s and the death in 2018 at 93 are in two or more sources each; the orchards, the single stakes as his own, the buyers abroad and the address visitors sought were found nowhere; the line on Renaissance as an addition after his death had no source.

changed.was: Condrieu's Viognier was once as often sweet as dry, and its steep granite terraces were hard to work and badly paid. The appellation was drawn in 1940, beside the single estate of Château-Grillet, which had been given an appellation of its own in 1936, but after the war the terraces emptied, and by the 1960s only a few growers tended the grape. The grower whose name the domaine carries took over his family's vines in that lean time and refused to let them go: he rebuilt fallen walls, replanted abandoned terraces and, as a leader of the local growers for many years, argued for a dry Condrieu that tasted of its place. When Viognier came into fashion in the 1980s and was planted from California to the Languedoc, his work was a large part of the reason there was a Condrieu left to rediscover. Coteau de Vernon, the old vines on the hill above the town, became the domaine's flagship, made to age rather than to drink at once. His daughter took charge in 1997, and he died in 2017. Most Condrieu is drunk within a few years; Coteau de Vernon was made to be kept.
changed.now: Sweet Condrieu was long the custom of the hill, and its steep granite terraces were hard to work. The appellation was drawn in 1940, beside the single estate of Château-Grillet, which had been given an appellation of its own in 1936. After the war the terraces emptied, and by the 1950s, as Inter Rhône tells it, the vineyard had all but vanished. The grower whose name the domaine carries held on to his vines through those lean years, and when he died in 2017 the obituaries credited him with saving Viognier from extinction. Inter Rhône dates the revival of the appellation to the 1980s and to the work of a handful of growers, and Viognier was later planted from California to the Languedoc. Coteau de Vernon, the old vines on the hill above the town, became the domaine's flagship, made to age rather than to drink at once. His daughter took charge in 1996. Most Condrieu is drunk within a few years; Coteau de Vernon was made to be kept, and it shows what the grape his family kept alive can become.
changed.why: Inter Rhône gives the appellation of 1940, Château-Grillet's of 1936, the near loss by the 1950s and the revival of the 1980s; Decanter and The Drinks Business give the death of 2017 and the credit for saving Viognier; the merchants give 1996 for the daughter; the rebuilt walls, the replanted terraces and the years leading the growers rest on one source or none.
